headline: Galápagos Daisies Show Evolution's Creative Genius
meta_description: Scientists discover that giant daisies in the Galápagos independently evolved the same leaf shape using different genes—revealing nature's flexible approach to…
summary_short: Galápagos giant daisies evolved identical heat-resistant leaves through entirely different genetic pathways, showing evolution's remarkable creativity.
body:
An international research team has uncovered a remarkable pattern in the Galápagos Islands: giant daisies repeatedly solved the same environmental challenge—surviving hot, dry conditions—by evolving identical leaf shapes, yet each time they did so using completely different genes. The discovery, published in Nature Communications, reveals that evolution doesn't follow a single blueprint. Instead of relying on one master gene, nature appears to improvise, tweaking different parts of a genetic network to produce similar physical outcomes. This is parallel evolution in action: the same solution, multiple times, through different genetic tools.

The research focused on Scalesia, the Galápagos giant daisies, a relatively young plant genus where every living species emerged within the past one million years. Despite this brief evolutionary history, these plants have adapted to strikingly different habitats—from humid highland forests to scorching lowlands. The most visually dramatic adaptation is the leaves: some are large and smooth, others deeply lobed with intricate, serrated edges. Those lobed leaves likely help plants survive by limiting water loss and releasing heat more effectively, yet the genetic mechanisms behind this shared trait had remained mysterious until now.

When researchers analyzed the complete genomes of every known Scalesia species, they found that lobed leaves had evolved independently several times across different branches of the family tree. Even more striking: each lineage had achieved this identical leaf shape through a different combination of genes within the same biological system controlling leaf development. The findings also suggest that new Scalesia species may currently be forming. Many isolated populations show large genetic differences and have been separated for extended periods, potentially representing distinct evolutionary lineages not yet formally recognized by science. This discovery carries real conservation implications: scientists argue that each isolated population should be managed as an individual unit, potentially transforming how the Galápagos' distinctive plants and ecosystems are protected.
quick_facts: Giant daisies evolved the same leaf shape through different genes
Every Scalesia species emerged within the past one million years
Parallel evolution: nature solving problems multiple ways simultaneously
New Scalesia species may be forming right now in isolated populations
